lessons.title: How to read a stock quote in 6 minutes
lessons.meta: Price, day change, volume, 52-week range, P/E and market cap — decode any stock quote line by line with examples.
body: Every stock quote answers six questions. Price is the last traded value — history, not a promise. Day change (points and percent) tells today's sentiment; check whether it moved with the index or against it.
Volume validates the move: big price change on thin volume is noise, on heavy volume it is institutional conviction. Compare today's volume with the 20-day average before reacting.
The 52-week high/low frames the price — near highs means momentum with overhead supply; near lows means either turnaround or terminal decline. Volume decides which.
P/E and market cap add valuation and size: a Rs 200 stock can be 'bigger' and pricier than a Rs 2,000 one. Learn both in our P/E and market-cap guides.
Do this now: open any holding in your watchlist and read all six fields aloud. If any number confuses you, tap through to its glossary page — that gap is your next lesson.

faqs.q: Why does the price differ across apps?
faqs.a: Snapshots refresh at different seconds and some show BSE vs NSE feeds. Live exchange data converges within ticks — use one source per decision.

lessons.title: What actually moves a stock price
lessons.meta: Earnings, interest rates, fund flows and sentiment — the four forces behind every price move, and which one dominates yours.
body: 1. Earnings. Over years, prices follow profits. Quarterly results reset expectations — guidance (what management promises next) moves stocks more than the reported quarter itself.
2. Interest rates. When the US Fed or RBI raises rates, future profits get discounted harder and growth stocks fall first. This single channel explains most 2022 damage — see Fed to FII.
3. Fund flows. FII selling and DII SIP buying tug Indian large-caps daily. Flows dominate months; earnings dominate years. Know which game your holding period plays — FII & DII explained.
4. Sentiment. Greed zones stretch multiples, fear zones compress them. Gauges like the Market Mood Index tell you which crowd you are trading against.
Do this now: pick your biggest holding and assign its last 10% move to one of the four forces. If you cannot, you are trading a story you haven't verified.

faqs.q: Good results but stock fell — why?
faqs.a: Expectations beat reality: the 'whisper number' exceeded guidance, or the market sold the broader sector. Price reacts to surprise, not quality.

lessons.title: 5 beginner mistakes that lose money (and fixes)
lessons.meta: Tips, averaging down, penny chasing, no stop-losses, all-in bets — the five classic beginner errors with a one-line fix each.
body: 1. Acting on tips. By the time a tip reaches you, early buyers need your exit. Fix: no position without your own two-line thesis — what it earns, why it grows.

2. Averaging down blindly. Adding to losers doubles exposure to whatever is going wrong. Fix: average only on pre-planned levels with fresh thesis intact — never to 'recover' fast. Our penny-stock screen shows why falling knives usually keep falling.
3. No position sizing. A 40% portfolio bet that halves needs a 67% gain elsewhere to recover. Fix: cap any single stock at 5–10% until you have three years of process.
4. No stop-loss or review date. Hope is not risk management. Fix: every buy gets an exit price (thesis broken) and a review date (thesis check).
5. Confusing bull markets with skill. Rising tides certify geniuses. Fix: benchmark every return against the Nifty 50 or S&P 500 — outperformance net of risk is the only grade.

faqs.a: For mechanics yes, for psychology no — real money triggers emotions paper never will. Start tiny with real capital and strict sizes instead.

lessons.title: P/E, ROCE, ROE and P/B in 10 minutes
lessons.meta: The only four ratios beginners need: what each measures, good vs bad values, and the two-minute combo that filters any stock.
body: P/E (price ÷ earnings) prices greed: under ~15 is value land, 15–25 normal, 30+ demands serious growth. Compare within sectors only. Full guide: P/E ratio.
ROCE (profit ÷ all capital) measures quality: sustained 15–20%+ marks a moat; under 10% destroys value after funding costs. Debt cannot flatter it — that is the point.
ROE (profit ÷ equity) measures shareholder compounding — but leverage inflates it, so always read it beside ROCE and debt levels.
P/B (price ÷ book value) suits banks and asset-heavy firms: below 1 often prices distress, not bargains, unless asset quality is clean.

The two-minute combo: P/E under 25 + ROCE above 15% filters most junk instantly. It is exactly the pairing behind the extension's AI Verdict — cheap plus efficient flags research candidates; expensive plus weak flags avoids.

faqs.a: ROCE for quality, P/E for price. One without the other misleads — great businesses at absurd prices still lose money.

lessons.title: How to screen 500 stocks down to 10
lessons.meta: A five-filter screening workflow — universe, quality, price, momentum, story check — that turns index lists into research watchlists.
body: Step 1 — Universe. Start from an index or collection (say, Nifty 500 or our defence list), not the whole market. Boundaries beat infinity.
Step 2 — Quality filter. Keep ROCE > 15%, positive operating cash flow, debt-to-equity < 1. This typically cuts two-thirds of names — correctly.
Step 3 — Price filter. Of survivors, keep P/E below sector median or PEG below 1.5. Quality you overpay for is just expensive quality.
Step 4 — Momentum sanity. Prefer stocks above their 200-day average with rising volumes; downtrends need turnaround evidence, not hope. Check 52-week position.
Step 5 — Story check. Read the last two concalls of the 10 survivors. One hour here saves lakhs: management evasion, auditor exits or pledged shares disqualify instantly.
Do this now: run the five steps on any collection page's stock table and save survivors as a tagged watchlist portfolio. Re-screen quarterly — screens rot as prices move.

faqs.a: Quarterly, after results season. Prices move daily but fundamentals print quarterly — match the cadence to the data.

lessons.title: ETF vs stock: which should you pick?
lessons.meta: When index ETFs beat stock-picking (core holdings) and when single stocks win (conviction) — plus the fee math that decides.
body: An ETF buys the whole basket: diversification, sub-0.3% fees and zero research burden. A stock buys one thesis: concentration, upside and the risk of being wrong.
Rule of thumb: core in ETFs, satellite in stocks. Index funds for the Nifty 500 / S&P 500 spine of your portfolio; 5–15 hand-picked stocks where you genuinely understand the business.
The fee math is merciless — a 1.5% yearly edge for active fees needs persistent outperformance few deliver. Check any fund's expense ratio before admiring its past chart.
Where to start: a Nifty 50 ETF plus a gold ETF hedge covers most beginners' core; add single stocks only after finishing Track 2's ratio lessons.

faqs.a: Yes — an index ETF mirrors its market, crashes included. Diversification softens single-stock risk, not market risk.

lessons.title: Read the market in 3 numbers: index, mood, breadth
lessons.meta: Index level, sentiment gauge and advance-decline breadth — the 60-second market check that prevents buying tops and selling bottoms.
body: 1. Index vs trend. Is the Nifty 50 (or S&P 500) above its 200-day average? Above means the tide still rises; below means respect cash. One line, no opinions.
2. Mood gauge. Check the Market Mood Index for India or Fear & Greed for the US. Extreme greed: tighten stops, book partials. Extreme fear: prepare buy lists, stagger entries.
3. Breadth. Read the advance-decline ratio: index up on 1:2 breadth is two giants masking 1,800 fallers — fragile. Index up on 2:1 breadth is participation — durable.
The 60-second routine: trend, mood, breadth — in that order, every morning. It will not predict anything; it will stop you from buying euphoria and selling panic, which is worth more than prediction.

faqs.q: Where do I see all three live?
faqs.a: The extension's Markets tab stacks the Market Mood gauge, whole-market breadth and index heatmap on one screen — the routine takes seconds.
